summary: Proposes an optional Proxy Mobile IPv6 extension to support Home Network Prefix renumbering. The base protocol does not say what happens when the prefix assigned to a mobile node must change, for example after a change of provider or topology.

eli5.summary: When your home address changes, this explains how the postal system keeps up while you move around.

subtitle: How a Proxy Mobile IPv6 network tells a device its home prefix has changed, without the device doing anything special.

tldr.problem: In Proxy Mobile IPv6 a mobile node keeps the same Home Network Prefix while it moves, but the base specification says nothing about what to do when that prefix has to change, for example after a switch of service provider or a change of network topology.
tldr.mechanism: The Local Mobility Anchor sends an Update Notification (UPN) to the Mobile Access Gateway with the new prefix. The gateway announces it to the node by Router Advertisement or DHCP and answers with an Update Notification Acknowledgement (UPA).
tldr.outcome: Prefix renumbering becomes an optional, defined extension of PMIPv6, with a soft mode and a hard mode for handling ongoing sessions.

today: RFC 8191 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2017. It has not been obsoleted or updated according to the metadata, and it describes an optional extension to PMIPv6 (RFC 5213).

sections.title: Why Prefixes Need to Change
sections.content:
In Proxy Mobile IPv6 (PMIPv6, RFC 5213) a Mobile Node (MN) gets a Home Network Prefix (HNP) when it first attaches, and builds its Home Address (HoA) from it. The HNP stays the same while the node moves, so ongoing communication tied to the HoA keeps working.

The base specification does not say what happens when the HNP itself must change. This document adds an optional extension for that case. It aims at HNPs that are not Provider-Independent (PI) prefixes, because the text notes that widespread use of PI addresses causes BGP scaling problems (RFC 7010) and that tools which make IPv6 renumbering simpler reduce demand for PI space (RFC 6879).
sections.eli5: Your street name can change. The base rules for travelling devices never said how to tell a traveller about that, so this document adds the missing steps.

sections.title: Usage Scenarios
sections.content:
The RFC lists three situations where renumbering may happen:

  • Scenario 1: the HNP set comes from a different ISP, and the PMIPv6 provider switches to another ISP.
  • Scenario 2: a provider runs several Local Mobility Anchors (LMAs), each serving its own HNP set, and the node moves to an LMA that does not inherit its assigned HNP set (RFC 6463).
  • Scenario 3: the provider rebuilds its network because companies split, merge, grow, relocate or reorganize.

Scenario 1 is the basic case: only the HNP changes and the serving LMA stays the same. In Scenarios 2 and 3 the situation can be more complex, for example when the serving LMA is switched.

In plain Mobile IPv6 the Home Agent actively tells the node about a new prefix (RFC 6275). In PMIPv6 the binding is normally triggered by the Mobile Access Gateway (MAG), so the LMA needs a way to start the update itself. RFC 5213 mentions this in its Section 6.12, but gives no solution.
sections.eli5: Sometimes the whole neighbourhood is renamed, sometimes you move to a different post office. In both cases someone has to tell you the new address.

sections.title: The Renumbering Procedure
sections.content:
When renumbering happens, the LMA MUST notify the MAG about the new HNP. The MAG MUST then announce it to the attached node, and both sides MUST update their routing state. The RFC reuses the asynchronous update mechanism of RFC 7077.

Same LMA. The serving LMA SHOULD start the operation and allocates a new HNP. It sends an Update Notification (UPN) to the MAG; if DHCP is used, the DHCP infrastructure MUST also learn the new HNP. The MAG MUST tell the node, either by a Router Advertisement (RA) or by allocating a new address inside the new HNP through DHCP. The node deletes the old HoA and configures a new one. Once that works, the MAG MUST update its binding and routing state and returns an Update Notification Acknowledgement (UPA), after which the LMA replaces the old HNP with the new one.

LMA switchover. The provider SHOULD update the LMA information in the MAG's profile. The MAG then registers with the new LMA as in RFC 5213, the new HNP arrives during that binding, and the MAG withdraws the old HNP and announces the new one, much as in the same-LMA case.
sections.eli5: The post office (LMA) tells the hotel front desk (MAG) the new address. The front desk tells you, you swap the address on your luggage, and the front desk confirms back to the post office.

sections.title: Session Connectivity: Soft and Hard Mode
sections.content:
Renumbering MAY break ongoing communication, so the RFC describes two ways to manage sessions.

In soft mode the LMA temporarily keeps the state of the old HNP after receiving the UPA. This lets it redirect packets to the node until the node reconnects its session and tells the Correspondent Node (CN) about its new HoA. The aim is less packet loss. The old binding SHOULD be marked, for example as a transient binding (RFC 6058), and the LMA MUST stop advertising routing information for the old HNP if that HNP is no longer anchored at this LMA.

In hard mode the LMA deletes the old HNP binding state once it receives the UPA and silently discards packets destined to the old HNP. Hard mode is RECOMMENDED when renumbering comes with an LMA switchover, because it keeps the protocol simple.
sections.eli5: Soft mode is like keeping mail forwarding on for a while after you move. Hard mode is like cutting off the old address right away, which is simpler but some mail gets lost.

sections.title: Message Contents
sections.content:
The RFC does not define new message types. It says how existing ones are filled in:

  • UPN: sent from LMA to MAG with the notification reason set to 2 (UPDATE-SESSION-PARAMETERS). It carries the HNP Option with the new HNP and the Mobile Node Identifier Option (RFC 4283), in either order.
  • UPA: acknowledges a UPN that had the (A) flag set. If the MAG could not renumber, the Status Code is 128 (FAILED-TO-UPDATE-SESSION-PARAMETERS), and what the LMA does next is specific to the provider.
  • RA: carries two Prefix Information Options (RFC 4861, RFC 4862). The first holds the old HNP with Preferred Lifetime set to 0. The second holds the new HNP with Valid and Preferred Lifetimes larger than 0.
  • DHCP: new addresses, such as the HoA, are generated from the new HNP, and the procedure is triggered by receiving the UPN (RFC 3315).
sections.eli5: No new kinds of letters are invented. The same old forms are reused, with the boxes filled in so they say: stop using this address, start using that one.

sections.title: Security and Other Issues
sections.content:
The UPN and UPA messages MUST be protected with security associations that give integrity and data origin authentication, as in RFC 5213 and RFC 7077. The LMA MUST follow the normal PMIPv6 procedure so that only an authorized HNP is assigned to the node, and the new HNP is for that node's exclusive use.

There is also a subtle RA detail. Per RFC 4862, an unauthenticated RA whose Prefix Information Option has a Valid Lifetime under 2 hours is ignored. So when the MAG deprecates the old HNP in an unauthenticated RA, the Valid Lifetime SHOULD be 2 hours with Preferred Lifetime 0. If the signalling between MAG and node is known to be legitimate, setting the Valid Lifetime to 0 MAY be acceptable.

Updating the node's DNS record may be needed to keep it reachable (RFC 3007), but that is out of scope. The document needs no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: Only trusted people may change the address book, and the old address is kept on the list for a short while so nobody can trick the hotel into throwing it away instantly.
